decks.title: Writing Skills — Part 1: The Formal Letter
goals: Lay out a formal letter in the CBSE format, part by part
Organise the body in three paragraphs: purpose, details, action
Write in a polite, formal register without slang or contractions
Write complaint, editor, order and enquiry letters within 100–120 words

slides.heading: Writing Skills — Part 1: The Formal Letter
slides.body_md: CBSE Class 10 English, **Section B (writing, 10 marks)**. You write one formal letter and one analytical paragraph, choosing A or B in each. This part teaches the letter; Part 2 teaches the analytical paragraph.

rows: complaint, letter to the editor, placing an order, or enquiry (choose A or B)
describe and analyse a chart, graph, table, map or set of cues (choose A or B)

visual.alt: Table of the two board writing tasks: a formal letter of complaint, to the editor, placing an order or of enquiry, and an analytical paragraph on a chart, graph, table, map or cues; each is worth five marks in about one hundred to one hundred and twenty words.
visual.caption: CBSE 2026-27, Section B: writing 10 marks.

slides.narration: Welcome to writing skills. In Section B you write two pieces worth five marks each: a formal letter, and an analytical paragraph. Each has a choice of two questions, and each should be about one hundred to one hundred and twenty words. Both are very scoring if you learn the format and plan for one minute before writing. In this part we build the formal letter.

slides.heading: Four kinds of formal letter
slides.body_md: The syllabus names four types. Each has one job, one kind of reader and one tone.

rows: report a problem and get it put right
raise a public issue and suggest solutions

visual.alt: Table of four formal letter types with their receiver, goal and tone: complaint, letter to the editor, placing an order and enquiry.

slides.narration: There are four kinds of formal letter in your syllabus. A complaint reports a problem and asks for it to be put right. A letter to the editor raises a public issue for readers of a newspaper. An order letter asks a supplier for goods, exactly. And an enquiry asks for information before you decide. Before writing, name the type, because it decides your opening and your tone.

slides.heading: The format, top to bottom
slides.body_md: Learn the eight parts in order. The **subject comes before the salutation**.

visual.alt: Flow of the eight parts of a formal letter from top to bottom: sender’s address, date, receiver’s address, subject, salutation, body, complimentary close, and name.
visual.caption: The CBSE format, top to bottom.

slides.narration: Here is the format, from top to bottom. Your address, then the date. Then the receiver’s designation and address. Then the subject line, and only after that the salutation, Sir or Madam. Then the body, in three short paragraphs. Then the complimentary close, yours faithfully, and finally your name, with your designation if you write for a school or a group.

slides.heading: Getting the format details right
bullets: **Addresses:** short, with the city and PIN code; use the names and places given in the question.
**Date:** in full, e.g. *27 October 2026*.
**Subject:** 5–10 words naming the problem or purpose, plus a reference if there is one.
**Salutation:** *Sir/Madam,* (or *Dear Sir/Madam,*).
**Close:** *Yours faithfully* (CBSE also accepts *Yours sincerely*), then the name.
slides.narration: A few details earn the format mark. Keep addresses short, and always use the names and places the question gives you. Write the date in full. The subject line should name the problem or purpose in a few words, with an order or invoice number if there is one. Begin with Sir or Madam, and end with yours faithfully, then your name.

slides.heading: The body: three paragraphs, three jobs
slides.body_md: Purpose → details → action. Keep each paragraph to two or three sentences.

rows: say why you are writing, with a reference
I am writing to… / I wish to bring to your notice…
facts, figures, effects, or the list of items/questions
The problem is… / Kindly let me know… / We require the following…
what you want done, by when; polite close
I request you to… / I look forward to an early reply.

visual.alt: Table of the three body paragraphs: purpose, details and action, with useful opening phrases for each.

slides.narration: The body has three paragraphs, and each has one job. The first says why you are writing, in one or two sentences. The second gives the details: the facts, the effects, the list of items or the questions. The third says exactly what you want done and by when, and ends politely. If you stick to this, your letter will be clear and within the word limit.

slides.heading: Formal versus informal register
columns:
**Avoid (informal)**

- *Hi! / Dear friend*
- contractions: *I'm, don't, can't*
- slang: *super upset, stuff, guy*
- demands: *Fix it right now!*
- *Yours lovingly*

**Use (formal)**

- *Sir/Madam,*
- full forms: *I am, do not, cannot*
- neutral words: *very disappointed, goods, delivery person*
- requests: *I request you to…*
- *Yours faithfully*
slides.narration: Register means the level of formality. A formal letter avoids greetings like hi, contractions like I am written with an apostrophe, slang, and demands with exclamation marks. Instead it uses full forms, neutral words, and polite but firm requests such as I request you to. Being polite does not mean being weak. A calm letter with clear facts is far more persuasive.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: planning a letter of complaint
slides.body_md: *Question:* Riya ordered a study table online (Order No. FH20817); it came with a cracked top and missing handles. Write to the Customer Relations Manager.
bullets: **Type and tone:** complaint; firm and polite.
**Subject:** *Complaint about a damaged study table (Order No. FH20817)*.
**P1 purpose:** ordered on 15 October, delivered damaged.
**P2 details:** crack along one edge; two handles and screws missing; paid in advance.
**P3 action:** replace within a week or refund ₹6,499; packing and invoice kept.
slides.narration: Spend one minute planning. Name the type and tone: a complaint, firm but polite. Write the subject line with the order number. Then jot one line for each paragraph. Paragraph one: what was ordered and that it arrived damaged. Paragraph two: the exact defects, and that she paid in advance. Paragraph three: the remedy she wants, with a deadline, and the evidence she has kept.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: the finished letter
slides.body_md:
14 Shanti Nagar  
Jaipur 302006

27 October 2026

The Customer Relations Manager  
Furnish Home Pvt Ltd  
Koramangala, Bengaluru 560034

**Subject: Complaint about a damaged study table (Order No. FH20817)**

Sir/Madam,

I am writing to complain about a study table I ordered from your website on 15 October. It was delivered yesterday in a damaged condition.

The tabletop has a deep crack along one edge, and two drawer handles and their screws were missing from the box. Since I paid the full amount in advance, this is very disappointing.

I request you to replace the table within a week or refund the full amount of ₹6,499. I have kept the packing and the invoice for your inspection.

Yours faithfully  
Riya Sharma
slides.narration: Here is the finished letter. Notice the format, part by part, and the subject line that the company can trace. The three body paragraphs follow the plan exactly: purpose, details, action. The language is formal throughout, with no contractions or exclamation marks. The whole letter is about one hundred and twenty words, including the format, which keeps it inside the limit.

slides.heading: Check: choose the subject line
slides.narration: Your turn. Four subject lines for a complaint about a faulty geyser. Which one tells the reader the purpose, the product, and gives a reference they can trace?

slides.heading: The letter to the editor
slides.body_md: You write to **The Editor**, but your real audience is the newspaper's readers and the authorities.
bullets: Open with the issue: *Through the columns of your newspaper, I wish to draw attention to…*
Paragraph 2: who is affected and how (facts, not anger).
Paragraph 3: practical suggestions for authorities **and** citizens.
Keep it about the public, not only your own inconvenience.
slides.narration: A letter to the editor is different from a complaint. You address the editor, but you are really speaking to the public and the authorities through the newspaper. So open with the issue, then show who is affected and how, with facts rather than anger. End with practical suggestions, both for the authorities and for ordinary citizens. That balance shows mature thinking.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a letter to the editor in key sentences
slides.body_md: *Question:* Late-night loudspeakers in your locality disturb students before the board exams. Write to the Editor, *The City Chronicle*, Nagpur.
bullets: **Subject:** *Late-night loudspeakers disturbing students*
**P1:** *Through the columns of your newspaper, I wish to draw attention to the noise from loudspeakers at late-night functions in our locality.*
**P2:** students cannot study or sleep; elderly residents and patients suffer; noise goes on past ten at night.
**P3:** strict enforcement of time limits; quick action on complaints; organisers to keep volume low and end on time.
slides.narration: Here are the key sentences for a letter to the editor about loudspeakers. The subject names the problem. Paragraph one uses the standard opening and states the issue. Paragraph two widens it beyond yourself: students, the elderly and patients, and the timing. Paragraph three offers two kinds of suggestions, one for the authorities and one for the organisers. The full model is in the practice bank.

slides.heading: Order and enquiry letters
columns:
**Placing an order**

- P1: we wish to order the following…
- P2: a **numbered list**: item, specification, quantity
- P3: delivery date and place, payment mode, discount

**Enquiry**

- P1: where you heard of it, what you are planning
- P2: specific questions as polite indirect questions: *Kindly let me know whether…*
- P3: request a brochure or terms
slides.narration: Order and enquiry letters are the easiest to score in, because they are short and factual. In an order, put the items in a numbered list with specifications and quantities, then give the delivery date, payment mode and any discount. In an enquiry, ask specific questions politely and indirectly, such as kindly let me know whether, and end by requesting a brochure.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: the body of an order letter
slides.body_md:
*We would like to place an order for the following books for our school library:*  
1. Oxford Student Atlas for India (latest edition) — 10 copies  
2. Wings of Fire by A. P. J. Abdul Kalam — 5 copies  
3. Concise English–Hindi Dictionary — 8 copies

*Kindly deliver the books by 10 November and ensure that they are in good condition. Payment will be made by cheque on delivery. Please allow the usual educational discount.*
slides.narration: Look at how compact an order letter can be. One sentence states the purpose. A numbered list gives each title, its edition, and the number of copies, so the supplier cannot misread it. Then three short sentences give the delivery date, the condition, the payment mode, and a request for a discount. Nothing else is needed, and the word count stays well within the limit.

slides.heading: Check: put the format in order
slides.narration: Check yourself. Eight parts of a formal letter are shuffled. Put them back in the order they appear on the page, from the top. Remember where the subject line goes.

slides.heading: Check: the right register
slides.narration: One more. Four possible closing sentences for a complaint. Only one is polite, firm and formal. Which would you sign your name under?

slides.heading: How your letter is marked
slides.body_md: Five marks, four criteria. Format alone is only one mark: content and expression earn the rest.

rows: Sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject, salutation, complimentary close and name, in order (deduct 0.5 for one or two missing or misplaced parts).
All the cues are covered with relevant, specific details; the purpose is clear in the first paragraph and the action requested in the last.
Three clear paragraphs, logical order, linking words and a polite, formal register throughout.
Grammar, spelling and punctuation are correct; within the word limit.

visual.alt: Table of the SOYL letter rubric: format one mark, content two marks, organisation and expression one mark, accuracy one mark, with what earns each.
visual.caption: SOYL rubric modelled on the CBSE marking pattern.

slides.narration: Here is how a letter is usually marked. One mark for the format, all parts in the right order. Two marks for content: every cue covered with specific details, a clear purpose and a clear request. One mark for organisation and expression: paragraphs, linking words and formal tone. And one mark for accuracy: grammar, spelling and the word limit.

slides.heading: Summary: the formal letter
bullets: Name the **type** first: complaint, editor, order or enquiry.
Eight-part format; the subject comes before *Sir/Madam*.
Body: purpose → details → action, two or three sentences each.
Formal register: full forms, polite requests, no slang or exclamations.
Use every cue in the question, and the names and addresses it gives.

visual.alt: Flow of the eight parts of a formal letter from top to bottom: sender’s address, date, receiver’s address, subject, salutation, body, complimentary close, and name.
visual.caption: The CBSE format, top to bottom.

slides.narration: To sum up. Decide the letter type first, because it sets your opening and tone. Lay out the eight parts in order, with the subject before the salutation. Write three short paragraphs: purpose, details, action. Keep the register formal, with full forms and polite requests. And make sure every cue in the question appears in your letter.

slides.heading: Exam tips: the formal letter
bullets: Plan for one minute: type, subject, one line per paragraph.
Tick off each cue from the question as you use it; missing cues cost content marks.
Do not invent new addresses or names: use the ones given (or write "Examination Hall" if told to).
Stay near 120 words: a long letter loses accuracy and time, not gains marks.
Common slips: no date; subject after the salutation; *Yours faithfully* misspelt; *Dear friend*; contractions.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Plan for a minute before you write. Tick off every cue in the question as you use it, because missing cues are the commonest way to lose content marks. Use the names and addresses the question gives. Stay close to the word limit. And watch the usual slips: a missing date, the subject placed after Sir or Madam, and faithfully spelt wrongly.

decks.title: Writing Skills — Part 2: The Analytical Paragraph
goals: Read a chart, graph, table, map or set of cues quickly and accurately
Write an introduction and a one-sentence overview of the main trend
Describe and compare key figures with accurate trend and comparison language
Draw a conclusion from the data without adding opinions

slides.heading: Writing Skills — Part 2: The Analytical Paragraph
slides.body_md: The analytical paragraph (5 marks, 100–120 words) asks you to **describe, compare and conclude** from a visual input or cues. It is not an opinion essay.

rows: complaint, letter to the editor, placing an order, or enquiry (choose A or B)
describe and analyse a chart, graph, table, map or set of cues (choose A or B)

visual.alt: Table of the two board writing tasks: a formal letter of complaint, to the editor, placing an order or of enquiry, and an analytical paragraph on a chart, graph, table, map or cues; each is worth five marks in about one hundred to one hundred and twenty words.
visual.caption: CBSE 2026-27, Section B: writing 10 marks.

slides.narration: Welcome to Part Two, the analytical paragraph. You are given a chart, a graph, a table, a map, or a set of cues, and you write one well-organised paragraph that describes the information, compares the important figures, and draws a conclusion. It is not an essay about your opinions. Think of yourself as a reporter explaining the data to someone who cannot see it.

slides.heading: Five moves of an analytical paragraph
slides.body_md: Every paragraph, whatever the input, makes the same five moves.

visual.alt: Flow of the five moves of an analytical paragraph: introduction, overview, key figures, comparisons and exceptions, and conclusion.

slides.narration: Every analytical paragraph makes five moves. First, an introduction: what the input shows, where and when. Second, an overview: the big picture in one sentence. Third, the key figures, grouped sensibly rather than listed. Fourth, comparisons and any exception that breaks the pattern. Fifth, a conclusion that follows from the data. Learn these five moves and you will never stare at a blank page.

slides.heading: Read the input for one minute first
slides.body_md: Before writing, find: the title and source, the axes or columns and their **units**, the period, the highest and lowest values, the biggest change, and anything that breaks the pattern.

visual.alt: Flow of five things to read on a chart before writing: title, axes and units, highest and lowest values, biggest change, and the odd one out.
visual.caption: Spend one minute reading before you write.

slides.narration: Before you write a word, read the input for one minute. Check the title, and what each axis or column measures, including the unit: lakh, per cent, millimetres. Note the time period. Then find the highest and lowest values, the biggest change, and the odd one out. These five or six facts are the skeleton of your paragraph.

slides.heading: The language of trends
slides.body_md: Match the word to the **shape and speed** of the change: *rose slightly* for 100 → 104, *soared* only for a dramatic jump.

rows: a fall, a decline, a drop
peaked at, hit a low of

visual.alt: Table of trend language: verbs, nouns and adverbs for going up, going down, peaks and lows, no change, and fluctuation.

slides.narration: Your marks for expression depend on precise trend language. For a rise, use rose, increased or climbed, and for a dramatic jump, soared. For a fall, use fell or declined, and for a sudden crash, plummeted. A peak is the highest point. Remained stable means no change, and fluctuated means up and down. Add an adverb, sharply, steadily or slightly, that matches the size of the change.

slides.heading: The language of comparison
slides.body_md: Rose **by** = size of change; rose **to** = final value. A difference between two percentages is in **percentage points**.

rows: twice / three times as many as
Twice as many students cycled as walked.
a quarter, a third, the majority
A quarter of the students walk.
It rose from 20 to 30 per cent, by 10 points.

visual.alt: Table of comparison language: by for the size of change, to for the final value, ratios, proportions, contrast words and percentage points.

slides.narration: Comparison language turns description into analysis. Use by for the size of a change and to for the final value. Use ratios like twice as many, and proportions like a quarter or the majority. Use whereas and in contrast to set two trends side by side. And when two percentages differ, say percentage points: from twenty to thirty per cent is a rise of ten points.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: reading a bar chart
slides.body_md: Visitors to the State Heritage Museum, 2019–2025 (lakh).
bullets: **Overview:** a collapse in 2020, then steady recovery beyond the 2019 level.
**Key figures:** 4.2 → 1.1 (about a quarter) → 1.8 → 3.5 (nearly double) → 4.8 → 6.1 (peak).
**Comparison:** 2023 overtakes 2019; 2025 is almost one and a half times 2019.

visual.alt: Bar chart of visitors to the State Heritage Museum: 4.2 lakh in 2019, 1.1 lakh in 2020, 1.8 lakh in 2021, 3.5 lakh in 2022, 4.8 lakh in 2023, 5.6 lakh in 2024 and 6.1 lakh in 2025.
visual.caption: Visitors to the State Heritage Museum, 2019–2025 (illustrative data)

slides.narration: Let us read this bar chart together. The unit is lakh visitors, from twenty nineteen to twenty twenty-five. The big picture: a collapse in twenty twenty, then a steady recovery that goes beyond the starting level. The key figures are the fall from four point two to one point one, the near doubling in twenty twenty-two, and the peak of six point one at the end.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: the finished paragraph
slides.body_md: *The bar chart shows the number of visitors to the State Heritage Museum between 2019 and 2025. **Overall, visitor numbers collapsed in 2020 but then recovered steadily, finally exceeding the 2019 level.** In 2019 the museum received 4.2 lakh visitors. This figure plunged to just 1.1 lakh in 2020, roughly a quarter of the previous year's total. Recovery was slow at first, with 1.8 lakh in 2021, before numbers nearly doubled to 3.5 lakh in 2022. By 2023 attendance (4.8 lakh) had overtaken the 2019 figure, and it went on rising to a peak of 6.1 lakh in 2025. In conclusion, the museum has more than recovered from its sharp fall.*
slides.narration: Here is the finished paragraph. The first sentence introduces the chart. The second, in bold, is the overview. Then the figures follow in time order, each with a comparison: roughly a quarter, nearly doubled, overtaken. The verbs vary: plunged, recovered, rising to a peak. And the conclusion sums up without inventing reasons, because the chart does not tell us why the numbers fell.

slides.heading: Check: pick the overview
slides.narration: Your turn. A town’s population rose from two lakh to five lakh in twenty years. Which sentence gives the big picture, rather than a detail, an opinion or a vague statement?

slides.heading: Tables and surveys: group, do not list
slides.body_md: A table may have ten or more numbers. Choose three or four that tell the story, and **group** them: what rose, what fell, what changed most, what stayed the same.

visual.alt: Table of how 400 students of a Pune school travel to school: walking fell from 35 to 18 percent, bicycles from 30 to 22, school bus rose from 20 to 28, private vehicles from 10 to 24, and public transport from 5 to 8 percent between 2016 and 2026.
visual.caption: Survey of 400 students, Vidya Niketan, Pune (illustrative data)

slides.narration: Tables tempt students to read out every number in order. Resist that. Instead, group the rows. In this travel survey, walking and cycling fell, while cars, two-wheelers and the school bus rose. Pick the biggest changes for detail: walking almost halved, and private vehicles more than doubled. Mention the small change, public transport, in one short clause.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a table in four sentences
bullets: **Overview:** *The clear trend is a shift away from walking and cycling towards motorised transport.*
**Falls:** *Walking almost halved, from 35 to 18 per cent, while cycling fell from 30 to 22 per cent.*
**Rises:** *Private cars or two-wheelers more than doubled, from 10 to 24 per cent, and the school bus rose from 20 to 28 per cent, becoming the most popular choice.*
**Conclusion:** *Students today depend far more on vehicles than they did a decade ago.*
slides.narration: Here is the table turned into four strong sentences. One overview sentence names the shift. One sentence groups the falls, and one groups the rises, each with figures and a comparison word: almost halved, more than doubled. The conclusion sums up the decade. Add an introduction and the public transport detail, and you have a full paragraph of about one hundred and twenty words.

slides.heading: Check: by or to?
slides.narration: Quick check. The price of tomatoes went from forty to sixty rupees. Fill in by for the size of the change and to for the final price. Then check your answer.

slides.heading: Maps, plans and cues
slides.body_md: For a **then-and-now map or plan**, pair each change and group by theme (education, water, roads…). For **cues**, use every cue once, link them logically, and add a balanced conclusion.

rows: senior secondary school up to Class 12
primary health centre in the village
mobile tower and a library with Wi-Fi

visual.alt: Table comparing facilities in Sundarpur village in 2006 and 2026: school, drinking water, health care, road and internet all improved.
visual.caption: Village development plan, Sundarpur (illustrative data)

slides.narration: Some questions give a map or plan of a place then and now, or a list of cues. For a then and now input, pair each old feature with the new one and group them by theme. Use the past for the old picture and the present or present perfect for today. For cues, use every cue once, link them with words like however and similarly, and finish with a balanced conclusion.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: from a then-and-now table to a plan
bullets: **Intro + overview:** Sundarpur, 2006 vs 2026; improvement in every area shown.
**Education:** school up to Class 5 → up to Class 12.
**Water and health:** one hand pump → piped water to 80% of homes; clinic 15 km away → health centre in the village.
**Road and internet:** kutcha track → paved road to the highway; mobile tower and a library with Wi-Fi.
**Conclusion:** *Clearly, Sundarpur has transformed.*
slides.narration: Here is a plan for the Sundarpur table. After the introduction and overview, group the changes into three themes: education, then water and health, then roads and the internet. Each theme pairs the old with the new, using linking words such as but, similarly and too. Finish with a short conclusion. The full model paragraph is in the practice bank.

slides.heading: Check: correlation is not cause
slides.narration: Think carefully about this one. If two figures rise together, can your paragraph say that one causes the other? Decide whether the assertion and the reason are true.

slides.heading: How the analytical paragraph is marked
slides.body_md: Content carries most of the marks: an overview and **accurate, selected** figures with comparisons. Opinions and invented reasons lose marks.

rows: Introduction naming the input, an overview of the main trend, key figures with correct units, and at least one comparison; a conclusion that follows from the data.
Logical order (overview → details → conclusion), varied trend and comparison language, linking words.
Grammar, spelling and figures quoted correctly; no opinions beyond the data; within the word limit.

visual.alt: Table of the SOYL analytical paragraph rubric: content three marks, organisation and expression one mark, accuracy one mark.
visual.caption: SOYL rubric modelled on the CBSE marking pattern.

slides.narration: Here is how the paragraph is usually marked. Three marks for content: an introduction, an overview, key figures with their units, comparisons, and a conclusion that follows from the data. One mark for organisation and expression, including varied trend language. One mark for accuracy, which includes quoting figures correctly and keeping out personal opinions.

slides.heading: Summary: the analytical paragraph
bullets: Read for one minute: title, units, period, highest, lowest, biggest change, exception.
Five moves: introduction → overview → key figures → comparisons → conclusion.
Precise trend words and adverbs; *by* vs *to*; percentage points.
Group and select; never list every number.
Stay inside the data — no opinions, invented causes or advice.

visual.alt: Flow of the five moves of an analytical paragraph: introduction, overview, key figures, comparisons and exceptions, and conclusion.

slides.narration: To sum up. Read the input for a minute before writing. Make the five moves: introduction, overview, key figures, comparisons and conclusion. Use precise trend and comparison language, including by and to, and percentage points. Select and group the figures instead of listing them all. And stay inside the data, with no opinions, invented causes or advice.

slides.heading: Exam tips: the analytical paragraph
bullets: Write **one** paragraph of about 100–120 words; a short title is optional.
Quote figures exactly, **with units**; check every calculation you mention.
Use the simple past for past years, the present for what the chart shows.
Do not start with *I* or with a general remark about the topic; start with the input.
Common slips: no overview; all numbers listed; *rose by* / *rose to* confused; opinions; wrong units.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Write a single paragraph of about one hundred and twenty words. Quote figures exactly, with their units, and check any calculation you mention, like doubled or a quarter. Use the simple past for past years. Begin with the input, never with I. And avoid the classic slips: no overview, listing every number, confusing by and to, and adding your own opinions.

notes.title: Writing Skills — Class 10 board notes

sections.heading: 1. The writing section at a glance
sections.body_md:
Section B of the CBSE Class 10 English paper includes **two writing tasks of 5 marks each**, each with an internal choice (A or B): a **formal letter** (complaint, letter to the editor, placing an order, enquiry) and an **analytical paragraph** on a chart, graph, table, map or set of cues. Each should be about **100–120 words**.

Plan for one minute before writing. Both tasks reward a fixed structure, accurate language and complete coverage of the cues.

rows: complaint, letter to the editor, placing an order, or enquiry (choose A or B)
describe and analyse a chart, graph, table, map or set of cues (choose A or B)

visual.alt: Table of the two board writing tasks: a formal letter of complaint, to the editor, placing an order or of enquiry, and an analytical paragraph on a chart, graph, table, map or cues; each is worth five marks in about one hundred to one hundred and twenty words.
visual.caption: CBSE 2026-27, Section B: writing 10 marks.

sections.heading: 2. Formal letter: format
sections.body_md:
Eight parts, top to bottom:

1. Sender's address (short, with PIN code)
2. Date (*27 October 2026*)
3. Receiver's designation and address
4. **Subject:** 5–10 words, with a reference number if any
5. Salutation: *Sir/Madam,*
6. Body: three paragraphs
7. Complimentary close: *Yours faithfully* (*Yours sincerely* also accepted)
8. Name, and designation if writing for a school or group

Use the names and addresses given in the question.

key_terms.definition_md: The greeting before the body: *Sir/Madam,* in a formal letter.
The phrase before the name: *Yours faithfully* / *Yours sincerely*.

visual.alt: Flow of the eight parts of a formal letter from top to bottom: sender’s address, date, receiver’s address, subject, salutation, body, complimentary close, and name.
visual.caption: The CBSE format, top to bottom.

sections.heading: 3. Formal letter: body and register
sections.body_md:
**Paragraph 1 — purpose:** why you are writing (*I am writing to complain about… / I wish to bring to your notice… / Through the columns of your newspaper…*).

**Paragraph 2 — details:** facts, figures and effects (complaint, editor); a numbered list of items with specifications and quantities (order); specific polite questions (enquiry: *Kindly let me know whether…*).

**Paragraph 3 — action:** what you want, by when, and a courteous close (*I request you to… / I look forward to an early reply.*).

**Register:** full forms (*do not*), neutral words (*goods, delivery person*), polite firm requests; no slang, contractions, exclamation marks or emotional demands.

key_terms.definition_md: The level of formality of language. Formal letters use a formal register.

rows: say why you are writing, with a reference
I am writing to… / I wish to bring to your notice…
facts, figures, effects, or the list of items/questions
The problem is… / Kindly let me know… / We require the following…

sections.body_md:
**Five moves:** introduction (what the input shows, where, when) → overview (the main trend in one sentence) → key figures, grouped → comparisons and exceptions → conclusion drawn from the data.

**Read for one minute first:** title and source; axes, columns and **units**; period; highest and lowest values; the biggest change; anything that breaks the pattern.

**For tables and surveys:** group rows (what rose, what fell) and select 3–4 key figures. **For maps or then-and-now plans:** pair old and new features and group them by theme. **For cues:** use each cue once, link them, and end with a balanced conclusion.

sections.heading: 6. Analytical paragraph: language
sections.body_md:
**Trends:** rose, increased, climbed, soared; fell, declined, plummeted; peaked at; remained stable, levelled off; fluctuated — with *sharply, steadily, gradually, slightly*.

**Comparison:** *by* (size of change) vs *to* (final value); *twice / three times as many as*; *a quarter, a third, the majority*; *whereas, while, in contrast*; **percentage points** for the difference between two percentages.

**Tense:** simple past for past data (*sales rose*), present for what the input shows (*the table shows*), *may / might* for cautious predictions.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Marks:** formal letter 5 + analytical paragraph 5 (Section B, CBSE 2026-27), each about 100–120 words with a choice of two.

**How marks are awarded:** letter — format 1, content 2, organisation and expression 1, accuracy 1; analytical paragraph — content 3, organisation and expression 1, accuracy 1 (SOYL rubric modelled on the CBSE pattern).

**Common mistakes — letter**
1. Missing date, or the subject placed after the salutation.
2. Informal openings and closes (*Hi*, *Dear friend*, *Yours lovingly*).
3. Cues from the question left out.
4. Contractions, slang and exclamation marks.

**Common mistakes — analytical paragraph**
1. No overview; every number listed in order.
2. Figures without units, or misquoted; *by / to* confused.
3. Personal opinions, invented causes, or advice to the government.
4. Exaggerated trend words (*soared* for a 4 per cent rise).

**Time:** about 12–15 minutes for each task, including one minute of planning and one minute of checking.

questions.solution_md: **Plan:** introduce the chart → overview (fall, then recovery beyond the start) → details in time order with figures (4.2 → 1.1 → 1.8 → 3.5 → 4.8 → 6.1) → comparisons (a quarter; nearly doubled; one and a half times) → conclusion. assets.caption: Visitors to the State Heritage Museum, 2019–2025 (illustrative data)

answer.model_answer_md: The bar chart shows the number of visitors to the State Heritage Museum between 2019 and 2025. Overall, visitor numbers collapsed in 2020 but then recovered steadily, finally exceeding the 2019 level. In 2019 the museum received 4.2 lakh visitors. This figure plunged to just 1.1 lakh in 2020, roughly a quarter of the previous year's total. Recovery was slow at first, with 1.8 lakh visitors in 2021, before numbers nearly doubled to 3.5 lakh in 2022. By 2023 attendance (4.8 lakh) had overtaken the 2019 figure, and it went on rising to a peak of 6.1 lakh in 2025, almost one and a half times the 2019 level. In conclusion, the museum has more than recovered from its sharp fall.

answer.model_answer_md: The bar chart presents the average rainfall in a coastal town in Tamil Nadu from June to December. In short, the town depends mainly on the October–November rains, and these two months account for well over half the rainfall shown.

questions.solution_md: More than half = **the majority**. (*Minority* = fewer than half.)

marking_scheme.step: Blank 1: majority

questions.stem_md: Arrange the parts of an analytical paragraph in the best order.

options.text_md: Overview: the main trend in one sentence
Key details with figures, in a logical order
Introduction: what the chart shows, place and period

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (e) → (a) → (d) → (c) → (b). Introduce → give the big picture → support it with figures → compare and note exceptions → conclude.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Arrange the sentences to form a coherent analytical paragraph about a school's solar panels.

options.text_md: Production was lowest in January at 800 units.
In June, however, output dipped slightly to 1,300 units.
It rose steadily to reach a peak of 1,400 units in May.
The bar chart shows the electricity a school's solar panels produced each month from January to June.
Overall, output increased as the days grew longer and sunnier.
In short, the panels worked best in late spring.

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (e) → (a) → (c) → (b) → (f). Introduction → overview → lowest point → rise to the peak → the exception (*however*) → conclusion. The linking words (*Overall, It, however, In short*) signal the order.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Match each trend phrase with what the graph shows.

match_right.text_md: stopped changing after a rise or fall
a gradual climb at a constant rate

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Choose trend words that match the **shape and speed** of the change.

marking_scheme.step: Each correct pair 0.5 mark (4 pairs)

questions.stem_md: True or false: a good analytical paragraph quotes every number in the chart, in the order they appear.
questions.solution_md: **False.** Select the **key** figures (highest, lowest, biggest change, exceptions) and group them; listing every number is description without analysis.

marking_scheme.step: Correct choice (False)

questions.stem_md: True or false: figures quoted in an analytical paragraph should carry their units (per cent, lakh, mm, tonnes).
questions.solution_md: **True.** A number without its unit is unclear and can lose the accuracy mark.

marking_scheme.step: Correct choice (True)

questions.stem_md: True or false: when describing data for past years (for example 2019–2023), the simple past is generally used.
questions.solution_md: **True.** Past data → simple past (*rose, fell, peaked*). Use the present for what the chart *shows* (*The chart shows…*) and for predictions or current facts.

marking_scheme.step: Correct choice (True)

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** An analytical paragraph should give an overview near the beginning.

**Reason (R):** Figures quoted in an analytical paragraph should carry their units.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true, but R (about units) does not explain why the overview comes early; the reason is that it gives the reader the main trend before the details.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (b)

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** If a chart shows that ice-cream sales and drowning cases both rose in summer, the paragraph should state that ice cream causes drowning.

**Reason (R):** An analytical paragraph may compare two sets of data shown together.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: two figures rising together does not prove that one causes the other; the paragraph should only say they rose together. R is true.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (d)

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** An analytical paragraph should begin by stating what the chart, graph or table shows.

**Reason (R):** An analytical paragraph needs a salutation and a signature, like a letter.

Choose the correct option.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: the introduction names the input, place and period. R is false: there is no letter format (a short title is optional).

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (c)

questions.stem_md: A table shows the number of trees planted in a district: 2021 — 12,000; 2022 — 18,000; 2023 — 15,000; 2024 — 30,000. Write an **introduction and overview** (two sentences) for an analytical paragraph.
questions.solution_md: Sentence 1 names the input, place and period. Sentence 2 gives the big picture: a general rise (12,000 → 30,000; 30 ÷ 12 = 2.5) with one exception (the 2023 dip). No details beyond what the overview needs.

answer.model_answer_md: The table shows the number of trees planted in the district each year from 2021 to 2024. Overall, planting increased over the period despite a dip in 2023, and the 2024 figure was two and a half times that of 2021.

marking_scheme.step: Introduction names input, place and period
Overview gives the main trend accurately (rise, with the 2023 dip)

questions.stem_md: In a survey, 120 students chose cricket, 60 chose football and 20 chose chess as their favourite sport. Write **two sentences** comparing the figures, using different comparison structures.
questions.solution_md: 120 ÷ 60 = 2 (*twice as many*); 20 ÷ 120 = 1/6 (*a sixth of*). Varying structures (*by far the most, twice as many as, a sixth of*) shows control of comparison language.

answer.model_answer_md: Cricket was by far the most popular sport, chosen by twice as many students as football. Chess, chosen by only 20 students, attracted a sixth of the number who picked cricket.

marking_scheme.step: Accurate comparison 1 (twice as many / double)
Accurate comparison 2 with a different structure (a sixth / far fewer)

questions.stem_md: A chart shows that the share of households in a city using LPG for cooking rose from 55 per cent in 2015 to 92 per cent in 2025, while the use of firewood fell from 30 to 3 per cent. Write a **concluding sentence or two** that stays within the data.
questions.solution_md: A conclusion sums up the overall change (LPG 92 per cent ≈ almost all; firewood 30 → 3 per cent) without inventing causes or giving advice the chart cannot support.

answer.model_answer_md: In conclusion, LPG has become the main cooking fuel for almost all households in the city, while firewood, used by nearly a third of homes in 2015, has almost disappeared.

marking_scheme.step: Summarises the main change accurately
Stays within the data; no invented causes or opinions

questions.stem_md: Monthly visitors to a hill station (thousands): March 20, April 45, May 80, June 75, July 15. In **40–50 words**, describe the main pattern and the most striking change.
questions.solution_md: Pattern: rise to a May peak (80 ÷ 20 = 4), a high plateau in June, then a sudden fall in July (75 → 15). The most striking change is the July drop, so it is described with a strong verb (*plummeted*).

answer.model_answer_md: Visitor numbers climbed sharply from 20 thousand in March to a peak of 80 thousand in May, four times the March figure. They stayed high in June at 75 thousand, but then plummeted to just 15 thousand in July, the lowest level of the five months.

marking_scheme.step: Rise to the peak with figures
June level and July fall with figures
Apt trend language; accurate; within limit

questions.stem_md: Two schools recorded the percentage of students scoring above 90 in Class 10 English: **School P** — 2023: 12%, 2024: 15%, 2025: 21%; **School Q** — 2023: 25%, 2024: 22%, 2025: 20%. In **80–100 words**, compare the performance of the two schools and draw a conclusion.
questions.solution_md: Introduction → overview (opposite trends) → School P with figures (+9 points) → School Q with figures (−5 points) → the changing gap (25 − 12 = 13; 21 − 20 = 1) → a cautious conclusion (*If these trends continue…*, *may*), which is a reasonable inference, not a certainty.

answer.model_answer_md: The data compares the share of Class 10 students scoring above 90 in English at two schools from 2023 to 2025. The two schools moved in opposite directions. School P improved every year, from 12 per cent to 15 per cent and then to 21 per cent, a rise of 9 percentage points. School Q, in contrast, began well ahead at 25 per cent but declined steadily to 22 and then 20 per cent. As a result, the gap between them narrowed from 13 points to just one. If these trends continue, School P may soon overtake School Q.

marking_scheme.step: Introduction and overview of opposite trends
School P described with figures
School Q described with figures
Comparison of the gap (13 → 1 point)
Cautious, data-based conclusion; accurate language

children.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** It should come before the salutation. In the CBSE format the subject line comes after the receiver's address and **before** the salutation.

questions.stem_md: Read a student's draft analytical paragraph on a bar chart of **metro ridership in a city (2021: 1.5 lakh daily riders; 2022: 2.4 lakh; 2023: 3.1 lakh; 2024: 3.0 lakh; 2025: 3.9 lakh)** and answer the questions.

**(a)** (a) It gives a personal opinion instead of introducing the chart.

**(b)** (d) the small dip in 2024 within an overall rise

**(c)** Overall, daily ridership grew strongly, from 1.5 lakh to 3.9 lakh, with only a slight dip in 2024.

Part (b)
Part (c)

questions.passage_md: Metro is very good and I use it every day. In 2021 there were 1.5 lakh riders. In 2022 there were 2.4 lakh riders. In 2023 there were 3.1 lakh riders. In 2024 there were 3.0 lakh riders. In 2025 there were 3.9 lakh riders. The government must build more metro lines everywhere.

options.text_md: It gives a personal opinion instead of introducing the chart.
